heading.en: A cold bulb and a hot bulb

hook.en: Measure the resistance of a cold 60 W filament bulb and you get less than 100 ohm. When it glows on 230 V its resistance is close to 900 ohm. *Temperature* changes resistance.
hook.kn: ತಣ್ಣನೆಯ 60 W ಬಲ್ಬ್‌ನ ರೋಧ 100 ಓಮ್‌ಗಿಂತ ಕಡಿಮೆ. 230 V ನಲ್ಲಿ ಉರಿಯುವಾಗ ಅದು ಸುಮಾರು 900 ಓಮ್ ಆಗುತ್ತದೆ. ತಾಪವು ರೋಧವನ್ನು ಬದಲಿಸುತ್ತದೆ.

say.en: Measure the resistance of a cold 60 watts filament bulb and you get less than 100 ohm. When it glows on 230 volts its resistance is close to 900 ohm. Temperature changes resistance. In this lesson: Use rho _T equals rho 0[1 plus alpha (T - T 0)].
Compare metals, alloys and semiconductors.
Recognise non-ohmic devices.

body.en: For metals resistivity rises with *temperature*, nearly linearly: $\rho_T = \rho_0[1 + \alpha(T - T_0)]$, α being the temperature coefficient of resistivity (copper: about 4 × 10⁻³ °C⁻¹). Hotter ions vibrate more, collisions are more frequent and τ falls. Alloys such as nichrome and manganin have high ρ and very small α, so they are used for heating elements and standard resistors. In semiconductors ρ falls as T rises, because the number of carriers n increases. Insulators have very large ρ.
body.kn: ಲೋಹಗಳಲ್ಲಿ ತಾಪ ಹೆಚ್ಚಿದಂತೆ ರೋಧಶೀಲತೆ ಹೆಚ್ಚುತ್ತದೆ: ρ_T = ρ₀[1 + α(T − T₀)]. ಮ್ಯಾಂಗನಿನ್‌ನಂತಹ ಮಿಶ್ರಲೋಹಗಳಲ್ಲಿ α ಬಹಳ ಕಡಿಮೆ. ಅರೆವಾಹಕಗಳಲ್ಲಿ ತಾಪ ಹೆಚ್ಚಿದಂತೆ ರೋಧಶೀಲತೆ ಕಡಿಮೆಯಾಗುತ್ತದೆ.

points.en: Metals: ρ increases with T (α positive)

narration.en: In metals, resistivity rises with temperature because collisions become more frequent. Alloys like manganin hardly change, so they make standard resistors. In semiconductors resistivity falls as temperature rises because more charge carriers are freed.

title.en: On the board: resistivity and temperature

narration.en: Resistivities span a huge range: about 10⁻⁸ ohm metre for metals, and above 10¹⁰ for insulators. For metals ρ rises almost linearly with temperature: ρ_T = ρ₀[1 + α(T − T₀)]. In a semiconductor ρ falls as it warms, because more charge carriers are set free. Example: 2.1 Ω at 27 °C and 2.7 Ω at 100 °C give α = 0.6 over 2.1 × 73, about 3.9 × 10⁻³ per degree. Ohm's law fails for devices like a diode: its V–I graph is curved and depends on the direction of V.

Resistivities span a huge range: about 10 to the power minus 8 ohm metre for metals, and above 10 to the power 10 for insulators. For metals rho rises almost linearly with temperature: rho _T equals rho 0[1 plus alpha (T - T 0)]. In a semiconductor rho falls as it warms, because more charge carriers are set free. Example: 2.1 ohms at 27 degrees Celsius and 2.7 ohms at 100 degrees Celsius give alpha equals 0.6 over 2.1 times 73, about 3.9 times 10 to the power minus 3 per degree. Ohm's law fails for devices like a diode: its V-I graph is curved and depends on the direction of V.

narration.en: For a metal ρ = ρ0[1 + α(T − T0)]: hotter atoms vibrate more and scatter electrons more often. Silver and tungsten change a lot; nichrome little; manganin hardly at all, which is why it is used in standard resistors. R = ρL/A. Values at 20 °C from the NCERT table.

body.en: *Ohm's* law is not a universal law. Some devices are non-ohmic: (a) V is not proportional to I (a lamp filament as it heats up); (b) the current depends on the sign of V, not just its size (a p-n junction diode); (c) the same current occurs at more than one voltage (GaAs).
body.kn: ಓಮ್ ನಿಯಮ ಸಾರ್ವತ್ರಿಕವಲ್ಲ. ಉರಿಯುವ ತಂತು, ಡಯೋಡ್ ಮತ್ತು GaAs ಗಳಲ್ಲಿ V ಮತ್ತು I ಅನುಪಾತದಲ್ಲಿರುವುದಿಲ್ಲ.

points.en: Depends on the sign of V (diode)
Same I at more than one V (GaAs)

narration.en: Ohm's law is not universal. A glowing filament, a diode, and gallium arsenide are examples where V and I are not simply proportional.

say.en: Let us solve this together. A silver wire has a resistance of 2.1 ohms at 27.5 degrees Celsius and 2.7 ohms at 100 degrees Celsius. Find the temperature coefficient of resistivity of silver.
alpha equals (R 2 - R 1)/[R 1(T 2 - T 1)].
= 2.7 minus 2.1/2.1 times 72.5 equals 0.6 over 152.25.
alpha is approximately 3.9 times 10 to the power minus 3 degrees Celsius to the power minus 1.
So the answer is About 3.9 times 10 to the power minus 3 degrees Celsius to the power minus 1.

problem.en: A nichrome heater on 230 V draws 3.2 A when first switched on at 27 °C and 2.8 A when steady. α for nichrome is 1.70 × 10⁻⁴ °C⁻¹. Find the steady temperature.

narration.en: Let us solve this together. A nichrome heater on 230 V draws 3.2 A when first switched on at 27 °C and 2.8 A when steady. α for nichrome is 1.70 × 10⁻⁴ °C⁻¹. Find the steady temperature.

say.en: Let us solve this together. A nichrome heater on 230 volts draws 3.2 A when first switched on at 27 degrees Celsius and 2.8 A when steady. alpha for nichrome is 1.70 times 10 to the power minus 4 degrees Celsius to the power minus 1. Find the steady temperature.
R 27 equals 230 over 3.2 equals 71.9 ohms; R T equals 230 over 2.8 equals 82.1 ohms.
T minus 27 equals (R T - R 27)/R 27 alpha equals 10.3 over (71.9 times 1.70 times 10 to the power minus 4) is approximately 840 degrees Celsius.
T is approximately 840 plus 27 equals 867 degrees Celsius.
So the answer is About 867 degrees Celsius.

say.kn: ಮ್ಯಾಂಗನಿನ್‌ನಂತಹ ಮಿಶ್ರಲೋಹಗಳಲ್ಲಿ alpha ಅತಿ ಕಡಿಮೆ: ಪ್ರಮಾಣಿತ ರೋಧಕಗಳಿಗೆ ಬಳಕೆ.

say.en: Ohm's law fails for diodes, filaments and GaAs.
say.kn: ಡಯೋಡ್, ತಂತು ಮತ್ತು GaAs ಗಳಿಗೆ ಓಮ್ ನಿಯಮ ಅನ್ವಯಿಸುವುದಿಲ್ಲ.

say.en: Next: Electrical energy and power.
